title: Max Bottega: Keeping Art Direction interesting in a procedurally generated world
speaker: Max Bottega
summary: Max Bottega, former lead environment artist on Cyberpunk 2077 and the sole 3D artist at Mac n Cheese Games, shares the environment-art tricks used to make a procedurally generated, destructible world look good on a small budget. The studio's action roguelike, in which the player evolves into monsters across five biomes, assembles levels from 100+ hand-dressed hex tiles. He covers kitbashing props from small per-biome sets, 'props on their own feet' blending with bases and clustered debris, keeping uniform variation with a few hero props per tile, drop-in wall meshes, and a multi-camera trick for keeping biome palettes consistent.

insights.claim: Procedurally generated environments often look random and unattractive because it is hard to encode visual logic into how a generator places things.
insights.detail: Bottega frames his talk around this problem: procedural environments tend to look completely random and not good. He set out to address it within a small budget using hand-dressed tiles and art-side tricks rather than smarter generation.
insights.quote: We know the problem with procedural when it comes to the environment it often looks like it is a completely random. And it doesn't often look good.

insights.claim: Bottega's studio generates its five-biome world by procedurally arranging a library of over 100 hand-dressed hex tiles covered in destructible props.
insights.detail: With a single 3D artist and a short timeline, the team built a library of tiles dressed by hand and let the procedural system arrange them. Because each tile got little individual time, the art tricks had to be fast and effective while still producing a dense environment that was a pleasure to destroy.
insights.quote: it is procedurally generated by procedurally arranging a library of effects that are pre-addressed. We basically have a library of ties we address by hand.

insights.claim: Kitbashing props from 3-4 small asset sets per biome lets a tiny team produce many varied props quickly while keeping each biome's identity distinct.
insights.detail: Instead of a limited library of unique single-piece props, each biome gets a few small sets whose pieces are smashed together into all of that biome's props. Pieces occasionally cross biomes, but are mostly kept isolated to preserve identity. Building the library is slow at first but then speeds work up dramatically.
insights.quote: we decided to create sets for each biome we have a set of 3-4 small sets. We combine them to create all the props that are in that biome.

insights.claim: Props placed into procedurally assembled tiles look integrated when each one carries its own ground base and a gradient of clustered small debris around it ('props on their own feet').
insights.detail: Bottega contrasts wargame-style models dropped on a flat plane with props that include a piece of ground. Each prop has three layers: the core asset, a per-environment base, and pebbles, grass and small bushes that diminish in size and number outward. He stresses clustering these, since nature does not distribute objects uniformly.
insights.quote: we use basically three blending elements. One is the core of the object. The assets that compose the prop. The second one is a base

insights.claim: To keep procedural scenes readable, most props should be uniform generic pieces that don't demand attention, with only one or two attention-grabbing 'hero' props per tile.
insights.detail: Bottega calls this 'uniform variation': a library where every prop is unique and eye-catching distracts the player. The team made small and medium generic props plus 3-4 hero pieces per set, and dressed each tile with one or two hero props surrounded by generic props, then grass or bushes to blend them in.
insights.quote: we take each tile and try to place one or two hero props and surround them with genetic props of the same volume

insights.claim: Walls on procedural tiles can be single self-contained low-poly meshes that already include ground-blending debris, so they work when dropped onto any tile without adjustment.
insights.detail: Walls were the exception to the hero/generic dressing rule. Each wall block contains everything needed to blend into the ground, such as pebbles or bones, so it can be slammed onto a tile and work out of the box, which matters because many must be placed and they must stay low-poly.
insights.quote: the logic is we just slam on the tile and they work out of the box. We don't have to adjust

insights.claim: Viewing all biomes side by side through one composite camera while tweaking materials keeps their colors and gradients compatible so no area feels like it is from a different game.
insights.detail: As a bonus trick, Bottega set up a single camera that collected five proportional camera slices, each looking at a different biome, and adjusted objects and materials while looking through it to keep the overall look aligned across biomes.
insights.quote: I took a single camera and used it to collect other five cameras that were proportionate to slices and each was looking at the different biome
